mod1.title: Safe Handling of Sharps
mod1.desc: How to identify, handle, and safely isolate needles, syringes, and sharp razors.
mod1.step1Title: Never touch needles directly with bare hands
mod1.step1Content: Always use tongs, a dustpan, or puncture-resistant thick gloves when handling suspected sharps.
mod1.step2Title: Do not recap or bend used needles
mod1.step2Content: Recapping causes most accidental pricks. Leave the needle attached to the syringe as found.
mod1.step3Title: Place immediately into a rigid container
mod1.step3Content: Drop sharps point-first into a thick plastic container or puncture-proof sharps box. Do not use plastic bags.
mod1.step4Title: If pricked, wash under running water immediately
mod1.step4Content: Wash with soap and water, let it bleed gently without squeezing, and visit a clinic immediately.
mod1.q1Question: What should you do if you spot a discarded syringe with a needle?
mod1.q1Opt1: Pick it up with your fingers and throw it away
mod1.q1Opt2: Use tongs or pick it up with a rigid container without touching
mod1.q1Opt3: Break the needle with your foot first
mod1.q1Explain: Always use tongs or a rigid container to avoid any puncture contact with needles.
mod1.q2Question: Is it safe to put loose syringes into a normal plastic polythene bag?
mod1.q2Opt1: No, needles easily puncture polythene and pierce your hands
mod1.q2Opt2: Yes, if the polythene bag is double-wrapped
mod1.q2Opt3: Yes, as long as you tie the bag tightly
mod1.q2Explain: Needles easily pierce thin polythene. Always use rigid, hard-walled containers.
mod1.q3Question: What is the first step if you accidentally get pricked by a needle?
mod1.q3Opt1: Suck the wound with your mouth
mod1.q3Opt3: Wash under running water with soap and visit a clinic immediately
mod1.q3Explain: Running water and soap clean the wound safely; prompt clinic care assesses post-exposure prevention.

mod2.title: Broken Glass and Sharp Metal
mod2.desc: Preventing deep cuts and lacerations from shattered bottles, tin cans, and scrap iron.
mod2.step1Title: Wear thick leather or cut-resistant gloves
mod2.step1Content: Standard cloth gloves offer zero protection against glass shards. Use heavy-duty work gloves.
mod2.step2Title: Sweep or scoop small shards instead of picking
mod2.step2Content: Use a brush and pan or a piece of cardboard to scoop tiny splinters of glass safely.
mod2.step3Title: Wrap sharp edges in thick newspaper or cardboard
mod2.step3Content: Before bagging broken glass or jagged tin sheets, wrap them securely so they cannot cut through bags.
mod2.step4Title: Keep tetanus vaccination up to date
mod2.step4Content: A booster dose every 5 to 10 years protects against life-threatening tetanus from rusted metal cuts.
mod2.q1Question: Which type of gloves best protects against broken glass and jagged tin cans?
mod2.q1Explain: Heavy leather or cut-resistant gloves provide real physical shielding against sharp edges.
mod2.q2Question: How should broken glass be disposed of before placing in a collection sack?
mod2.q2Opt1: Wrapped inside thick newspaper or cardboard
mod2.q2Opt2: Crushed into smaller powder with bare hands
mod2.q2Opt3: Thrown loosely at the bottom of the sack
mod2.q2Explain: Wrapping glass in thick paper prevents shards from puncturing sacks and cutting handlers.
mod2.q3Question: Why is a cut from rusted metal especially dangerous?
mod2.q3Opt3: It carries a serious risk of tetanus infection
mod2.q3Explain: Rusted metal wounds carry bacteria that cause tetanus. A medical tetanus booster is critical.

mod3.title: Batteries and E-Waste
mod3.desc: Safely identifying lithium batteries, preventing fire hazards, and avoiding chemical leakage.
mod3.step1Content: Any bloated phone or gadget battery is a fire hazard. Never puncture, bend, or press it.
mod3.step2Title: Tape the metal terminals of batteries
mod3.step2Content: Apply plastic adhesive tape over battery terminals to prevent short-circuits and sparks in your bag.
mod3.step3Title: Store in a dry, cool place away from flammable scrap
mod3.step3Content: Keep batteries segregated from dry paper, cardboard, and textiles that catch fire easily.
mod3.step4Title: Never burn batteries or cables with plastic coating
mod3.step4Content: Burning batteries releases toxic lithium, lead, and acid fumes that cause permanent lung damage.
mod3.q1Question: What does a swollen or puffy lithium battery indicate?
mod3.q1Opt3: It is damaged and can catch fire or explode
mod3.q1Explain: Swelling is caused by trapped flammable gas inside the cell. It must be handled with extreme care.
mod3.q2Question: How can you prevent batteries from sparking against each other in your collection bag?
mod3.q2Opt2: Cover the metal contact points with tape
mod3.q2Opt3: Tie them together tightly with metal wire
mod3.q2Explain: Taping the terminals insulates contacts and prevents dangerous short circuits.
mod3.q3Question: What is the health danger of burning plastic-coated copper cables to extract wire?
mod3.q3Opt1: Releases toxic fumes that severely damage lungs
mod3.q3Opt3: Has no health danger at all
mod3.q3Explain: Burning PVC coating releases dioxins and toxic gases that cause severe respiratory poisoning.

mod4.title: Chemical Containers
mod4.desc: Safe handling of pesticide bottles, acid jugs, solvents, and pressurized aerosol cans.
mod4.step1Title: Check for danger symbols and skull marks
mod4.step1Content: Look for hazard warning symbols (flame, skull, corroding metal) before handling unfamiliar cans.
mod4.step2Title: Never sniff or inhale open chemical bottles
mod4.step2Content: Chemical vapors can cause instant dizziness, burns to the nasal passage, or unconsciousness.
mod4.step3Title: Do not mix unknown liquids together
mod4.step3Content: Mixing bleach with acid or ammonia produces deadly chlorine gas that suffocates in seconds.
mod4.step4Title: Keep pressurized spray cans away from heat and direct sunlight
mod4.step4Content: Aerosol cans can explode like grenades when heated above 50°C or struck with a hammer.
mod4.q1Question: What should you do if you find a container with a skull & crossbones symbol?
mod4.q1Opt1: Open it to check what is inside
mod4.q1Opt2: Treat it as toxic poison, avoid skin contact, and isolate it
mod4.q1Opt3: Rinse your face with the liquid
mod4.q1Explain: The skull symbol indicates acute poison or toxicity. Never touch without protective equipment.
mod4.q2Question: Why should you never mix leftover liquids from different cleaning bottles?
mod4.q2Opt3: They can react and generate lethal poisonous gas
mod4.q2Explain: Common cleaning chemicals can react violently to create toxic chlorine or chloramine gas.
mod4.q3Question: What danger do discarded pressurized spray cans present on a hot day?
mod4.q3Opt1: They can explode under heat and pressure
mod4.q3Explain: Aerosol propellant expands in heat and can rupture the metal can violently.

mod5.title: Medical and Bio Waste
mod5.desc: Recognizing clinical waste bags, soiled materials, and avoiding biological infection.
mod5.step1Title: Recognize yellow and red biohazard bags
mod5.step1Content: Hospitals and clinics use yellow or red bags marked with the biohazard symbol for infectious waste.
mod5.step2Title: Do not sort through biomedical waste bags
mod5.step2Content: Never open, tear, or salvage items from clinical waste. Report it to sanitation authorities immediately.
mod5.step3Title: Treat all blood-stained material as potentially infectious
mod5.step3Content: Viruses like Hepatitis B and C can survive dried on cotton bandages and cloth for days.
mod5.step4Title: Wash hands with soap thoroughly before eating or touching your face
mod5.step4Content: Sanitation hygiene is your strongest protection against accidental bacterial and viral infection.
mod5.q1Question: What kind of waste is typically found in yellow and red hospital bags?
mod5.q1Opt1: Infectious bio-medical waste that should never be scavenged
mod5.q1Explain: Yellow and red bags contain hazardous clinical waste that must only be treated in authorized facilities.
mod5.q2Question: How long can dangerous blood-borne viruses survive on contaminated materials?
mod5.q2Explain: Hepatitis B virus can remain infectious on environmental surfaces for at least 7 days.
mod5.q3Question: What should you do if an illegal pile of medical waste is dumped in your sorting area?
mod5.q3Opt1: Sort out the plastic tubes with bare hands
mod5.q3Opt2: Do not touch it, warn colleagues, and report via the app
mod5.q3Opt3: Burn the entire pile on the street
mod5.q3Explain: Report hazardous clinical dumping immediately so municipal teams can handle it with biosecurity protocols.
